summary:
Ecuador provides legal gender recognition on a self-determination basis. The 2016 Gender Identity Law permits change of legal gender and birth name on identity documents without surgery, and the December 2023 reforms to the Organic Law on Identity Management and Civil Data, regulated by a decree issued by President Daniel Noboa on 11 June 2024, streamlines the civil-registry procedure for changing name and sex or gender marker, which is the operative route for recognition.

The Constitutional Court has extended that route beyond adults. Rulings in 2024 and 2025 allowed trans adolescents to change name and sex on official records and publicly rebuked the National Assembly for stalling implementation of trans-rights legislation; an April 2026 report describes the adolescent ruling as opening a path for others seeking legal recognition.

The constitutional footing is explicit. Article 11 of the 2008 Constitution binds the state to respect differences of ethnicity, nationality, social and generational standing and gender, as well as sexual orientation and identity, forming the non-discrimination foundation for LGBTI rights in a secular, multinational state. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1997, when Constitutional Tribunal Case No. 111-97-TC struck Article 516 of the Penal Code, and the 1998 Constitution made Ecuador the first country in the Americas to bar discrimination based on sexual orientation.

Enforcement of those protections is uneven. A 2011 US State Department human rights report found that the right of LGBT community members to equal access to formal education was frequently violated, that gay, lesbian and transgender people continued to suffer discrimination from public and private bodies, and that LGBT groups claimed police and prosecutors did not thoroughly investigate deaths of LGBT individuals. Reporting from January 2024 describes violence against LGBTQ Ecuadorians increasing amid the country's internal armed conflict.

The gravest documented risk is detention. Ecuador's prisons are almost universally male, and trans women are held in male spaces where they face gender-identity discrimination, unsafe placement, sexual violence, forced suppression of gender expression and barriers to health care. Silueta X, through its PrisioTrans program, records a trans woman, Helen Maldonado, dying during the November 2021 massacre at Penitenciaria del Litoral while held in a male prison space; a 2022 complaint over cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment of trans women in Lago Agrio; 2024 allegations of forced head-shaving, beatings and violence targeting breast and body implants; and the 2026 death in state custody of a 23-year-old trans woman at the El Encuentro maximum-security prison, which drew calls for an independent investigation.

A Pulitzer Center investigation corroborates the placement pattern. The last prison census counted 73 trans women across all Ecuadorian prisons, a figure the organisation Fundacion Vivir Libre says understates the real number, and trans women are placed in male pavilions. A Venezuelan trans woman detained in August 2023 at Penitenciaria del Litoral was sent to a male pavilion rather than the prioritaria pavilion reserved for vulnerable populations, where many gender-diverse inmates are held, and received no medical examinations or HIV treatment there. Placement operates by birth sex and legal sex, with protective placement applied unevenly.
tangentialFactors:
Same-sex marriage has been legal since 2019, but Article 68 of the Constitution limits adoption to different-sex couples, and on 14 August 2026 new adoption legislation passed 118-0 explicitly prohibiting single and same-sex couples from adopting. The Constitutional Court had ordered the Civil Registry in 2018, by 5-3 with one abstention, to register the daughter of the same-sex couple Helen Bicknell and Nicola Rothon, a precedent for state recognition of same-sex families that the later statute constrains.

Conversion practices involving torture are explicitly criminalised: Article 151 of the Penal Code, amended in 2014, treats conversion therapy as equivalent to torture and carries 7 to 10 years' imprisonment, yet as of 2023 hundreds of clinics still promote it. Clinics have also confined young people against their will, including the daughter of parents who unsuccessfully sought her release.

The public climate contains both mobilisation and official sanction. Pride marches have been authorised in all major cities with police protection and official participation; a 2011 Guayaquil march included a vice prefect, a city councillor and a National Assembly member, attendance reached about 20,000 in Guayaquil in 2017 and over 18,000 in Quito in 2018, and the Presidential House was lit in rainbow colours in June 2017. In 2013 presidential candidate Nelson Zavala was fined more than $3,000 and barred from office for a year for calling gay people sinners and immoral. Diane Marie Rodríguez Zambrano became the first openly transgender candidate in 2013 and the first transgender lawmaker in 2017. The age of consent is 14 regardless of gender or sexual orientation.
localsOnly:
Residents change name and sex or gender marker once at the civil registry under the June 2024 reglamento, without surgery or judicial approval. Outright International's country overview, updated 12 March 2026, notes that legal gender recognition has been available since 2016 but was not available to under-18s before the Constitutional Court's adolescent rulings.

PrisioTrans does not press a single placement rule for detained trans people. It advocates individualised housing decisions under international standards that weigh gender identity, safety, the detainee's own assessment and informed consent, and cites a July 2016 government decision to develop protocols for LGBT people deprived of liberty.

Residents also face documented gaps in education access and in investigative response: the 2011 US State Department report recorded equal-access-to-education violations affecting LGBT community members, discrimination by public and private bodies, and LGBT group claims that police and prosecutors did not thoroughly investigate deaths of LGBT individuals.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved in the source inventory: whether the 2016 law's exclusion of under-18s has been formally repealed by the 2024 and 2025 Constitutional Court rulings or operates alongside them as an administrative practice.

Not sourced: whether Ecuador's criminal law provides an aggravating circumstance for bias-motivated violence against trans people, as distinct from the non-discrimination principles in Article 11 of the Constitution.

Not sourced: whether the adoption statute passed on 14 August 2026 has been challenged before the Constitutional Court, and its status on challenge.

Unresolved: the currency of the prison census figure of 73 trans women and the true size of the trans detained population, which Fundacion Vivir Libre states is substantially higher; also unresolved is the practical enforcement record of the Article 151 conversion-therapy prohibition despite hundreds of clinics promoting the practice as of 2023.

Not sourced in this inventory: entry, visa and border-screening treatment of passports bearing a changed gender marker, and any requirement to present birth certificates or court orders at Ecuadorian ports of entry.
